newsitem.title: FRANCE: France prepared to send troops quickly to Zaire.
newsitem.headline: France prepared to send troops quickly to Zaire.

text.p: France was prepared to send 600 paratroopers to Zaire within 24 hours of U.N. approval for a multinational force to help starving refugees and have 600 more there a day later, defence officials said on Wednesday.
But French officials said it was essential that the United States, which Paris believes will quickly approve the force, should commit its own troops on the ground to the mission.
"The United States must participate. The force must include (European, African and American) elements on the ground," government spokesman Alain Lamassoure said.
Army officers said the first French detachment which could go within 24 hours was from the Eighth Marine Infantry Parachute Regiment (8th RPIMa) based in Castres, southwestern France.

The unit recently served in ex-Yugoslavia and in Africa itself, restoring order and shoring up a government allied to Paris when the local army mutinied in the Central African Republic earlier this year.

The second 600 men, who could be in Zaire within 48 hours of receiving orders, would be drawn from a sister regiment, the 3rd RPIMa, also made up of professionals with vast experience in Africa, the officers said.
"In fact, such detachments are always ready. It's a coincidence that this time the first and second wave units are particularly well adapted to the mission," one officer said.
The troops would be flown from metropolitan France with weapons, rations and ammunition for several days under an existing alert system.

Armoured personnel carriers, if needed, could be flown in from the Central African Republic, the officers said. They declined comment when asked if helicopter gunships would be available to provide cover for humanitarian supply convoys.

Officials were also vague about where the proposed multinational force would muster. But they said Entebbe airport in Uganda or one of two French airfields in the Central African Republic could be the main base for the operation and the airlift of equipment and supplies required for the mission.
They said much still remained to be determined, including the precise mission at hand and especially the whereabouts of up to 1.2 million Rwandan refugees and displaced Zaireans.
"No one knows what's happening in the field. It's the rainy season and even American satellites are useless. Until we send scouts there, we won't know," one officer said.
He denied that a light aircraft which flew over Goma airfield on Wednesday drawing Tutsi rebel fire was a French military aircraft.
The officer played down opposition from the Tutsis to a Frech presence in the proposed force, saying France's position in the area was better than generally reported by the media.

Rwanda and the Rwandan-backed Tutsi rebels have voiced opposition to French military involvement in the operation, accusing Paris of backing the former Hutu rulers in Rwanda who were overthrown in 1994 after a massacre of Tutsis.

Most of the refugees in eastern Zaire are Hutus who fled Rwanda in 1994 when rebels of the Tutsi minority ousted the Hutu-dominated government which had orchestrated the genocide of hundreds of thousands of Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
Paris says its virtually unilateral intervention in 1994 was responsible for stopping the slaughter of Tutsis.
Lamassoure, commenting on the Zaire situation, told reporters on Tuesday that President Jacques Chirac had told his cabinet: "The time for unilateral interventions is over."
